title: Meta in depth
summary: How Meta's ad system actually decides who sees your ads: structure, objectives, conversion events, audiences, automation, learning, budgets and bidding. Button names change often, so this module teaches the principles that stay true, with worked examples you can apply in whatever the current Ads Manager looks like. The last lesson shows how to read the reports and make the daily call with the starting kill, hold and scale rules.

lessons.title: Campaign structure and objectives
objectives: By the end you can explain what is set at campaign, ad set and ad level.
You can choose an objective based on the event you want and the data you have.
You can spot a structure that splits budget too thin to learn.
You can build a campaign click by click and work out how many ad sets your budget can feed.

steps.h: Meta finds people who do what you ask for
steps.p: Meta's delivery system shows your ad to the people it predicts are most likely to take the action you optimise for. If you ask for clicks, it finds clickers. If you ask for deposits, it looks for depositors. Your structure and objective are how you ask.

d.b: You get what you optimise for

steps.say: Here's the most important idea in this module. Meta's delivery system shows your ad to the people it predicts are most likely to take the action you optimise for. Ask for clicks, and it finds clickers. Ask for deposits, and it looks for depositors. Your structure and objective are how you ask. You get what you optimise for, not what you hope for.

steps.p: Every Meta campaign has three levels. Knowing which setting lives where saves you from editing the wrong thing and resetting learning by accident. Exact options move between levels over time, so check the current Ads Manager.

rows: Objective, special ad category, campaign budget if used
Conversion event, audience, placements, budget, schedule

steps.say: Every Meta campaign has three levels, and each has its own job. Read the table. At campaign level you set the objective, any special ad category, and a campaign budget if you use one. At ad set level you set the conversion event, audience, placements, budget and schedule. At ad level, the creative, copy, link and tracking parameters. Knowing where each setting lives saves you from editing the wrong thing and resetting learning by accident. Options move over time, so check the current Ads Manager.

steps.h: One campaign, two ad sets, a few ads
steps.p: The starting structure as a picture. One campaign holds the objective. Two ad sets with clearly different audiences each hold three or four ads. Clicks go to your lander, and the paid event comes back as a signal.
steps.say: Here's the starting structure as a picture. Follow the lines. One campaign holds the objective, here Sales, and feeds budget to two ad sets with clearly different audiences, one broad and one interests. Each holds three or four ads. Clicks go to your lander, the lander leads to the broker sign-up, and the registration event comes back as a signal. Notice the last arrow: that signal returns to the campaign, which is how Meta learns.

steps.p: Meta groups objectives by outcome. At the time of writing they are roughly the six below. Names and groupings change; check the current Ads Manager before you build.
steps.say: Meta groups objectives by outcome. At the time of writing there are roughly six, shown on these cards. Awareness, for reach and memory, not actions. Traffic, for clicks or landing page views. Engagement, for messages, video views and interactions. Leads, for forms, calls and sign-ups. App promotion, for installs and in-app events. And Sales, for purchases and other conversions. Names and groupings change, so check the current Ads Manager before you build.

steps.p: A traffic objective finds people who click a lot. A conversion objective, such as Leads or Sales optimised for a website event, finds people who complete that event. For affiliate offers, cheap clicks rarely mean cheap deposits.

a.title: Traffic objective
items: Good for warming a new pixel

steps.say: Compare the two columns. A traffic objective finds people who click a lot. You get the cheapest clicks, but many accidental taps, and Meta learns who clicks. It can help warm a new pixel. A conversion objective, like Leads or Sales optimised for a website event, costs more per click but brings fewer, better visitors, and Meta learns who converts. It does need a working event. For affiliate offers, cheap clicks rarely mean cheap deposits.

steps.p: Example: a Traffic campaign gets clicks at $0.15 but only 0.5% register. A conversion campaign gets clicks at $0.40 and 3% register. Divide cost per click by registration rate to get cost per registration.
steps.more: Worked example. Traffic: $0.15 ÷ 0.005 = $30 per registration. Conversion: $0.40 ÷ 0.03 = $13.33 per registration. The click was more than twice as expensive, yet each registration cost less than half. This pattern is common in trading and iGaming, but not guaranteed, so test it with your own data.
steps.say: Here's why cheap clicks can cost more. In this example, a traffic campaign gets clicks at fifteen cents, but only half a percent register. That's thirty dollars per registration. A conversion campaign pays forty cents per click, a C P C more than twice as high, but three percent register. Look at the equation: forty cents divided by three percent is thirteen dollars thirty three per registration, less than half. This pattern is common in trading and iGaming, but not guaranteed, so test it with your own data.

steps.p: Work backwards from the action that makes you money, then move up only as far as your data forces you to. The deeper the event, the better the people, as long as there is enough volume.
d: If not, step one event up
steps.more: If you cannot track the paid event yet, fix tracking before you choose the objective. Full setup: Tracking setup lab module. If you can track it but get fewer than a handful a week, optimise one step higher and keep judging on the paid event.
steps.say: How do you choose the objective? Work backwards from the action that makes you money. Follow the steps. Name the paid event. Can you track it? If not, fix tracking first. Do you get enough volume? If yes, optimise for it. If not, step one event up the funnel, and keep judging on the paid event. The deeper the event, the better the people, as long as there's enough volume.

steps.h: Special ad categories are not optional
steps.p: If your ad promotes credit, and in some regions other financial products, you must declare the special ad category at campaign level. Targeting options are reduced. Declaring it honestly protects your account; hiding it gets ads rejected and accounts restricted.

d.text: Declare special ad categories where they apply. Check the current list for your geo.

steps.h: Too many ad sets starve each other
steps.p: Example: $50 a day split across 10 ad sets is $5 each. At a $20 cost per conversion, each ad set gets about 1.75 conversions a week. That is far too few for Meta to learn who your converters are.
steps.more: Worked example. $5 a day × 7 days = $35 a week per ad set. $35 ÷ $20 = 1.75 conversions. Put the same $50 into two ad sets and each gets $175 a week, or about 8.75 conversions. Still not a lot, but each ad set now has five times more signal. On small budgets, fewer ad sets almost always learn faster.

d.label: conversions per ad set per week
d.note: Example. $5 a day at $20 per conversion.

steps.say: Too many ad sets starve each other. Here's an example. Fifty dollars a day split across ten ad sets is five dollars each. That's thirty five dollars a week per ad set. At twenty dollars per conversion, each one gets about one point seven five conversions a week, the number on screen. That's far too few for Meta to learn. Put the same fifty dollars into two ad sets, and each gets about eight point seven five, five times more signal.

steps.h: How many ad sets your budget can feed
steps.p: The starting rule plans 3 × target CPA for each ad set so it can reach the kill and scale checks. Example: $50 a day for 6 days, target $30. $300 ÷ $90 is about 3 ad sets.
steps.more: Worked example. $50 × 6 = $300. 3 × $30 = $90 per ad set. $300 ÷ $90 = 3.3, so run 3 ad sets, not 10. With 10 ad sets each would get $30, which is only 1 × target, too little to apply even the zero-conversion kill rule at 2 × target. Full rule card: Budget and kill rules module.
steps.say: So how many ad sets can your budget feed? The starting rule plans three times your target C P A, cost per acquisition, for each ad set, so it can reach the kill and scale checks. Look at the equation. Example: fifty dollars a day for six days is three hundred dollars. Three times a thirty dollar target is ninety per ad set. Three hundred divided by ninety is about three point three, so run three ad sets, not ten.

steps.p: Example structure for a new offer and geo on a modest budget. One campaign, a small number of ad sets with clearly different audiences, and a few ads in each. Simple structures are easier to read.

Hiding a special ad category, so declare it honestly. Random names, so use one pattern everywhere. And editing at the wrong level, so know what lives where.

lessons.title: Conversion events and signal
objectives: By the end you can map your funnel steps to Meta events.
You can estimate the budget an event needs to give Meta enough signal.
You can explain why pixel plus Conversions API with deduplication gives better data.
You can read a server event and confirm deduplication with a real test conversion.

steps.h: The event is your most important setting
steps.p: The optimisation event tells Meta what a good result looks like. Choose an event that is too shallow and Meta finds people who do cheap things. Choose one that is too rare and Meta cannot learn. Your skill is finding the right depth.
steps.say: The optimisation event tells Meta what a good result looks like. Choose an event that's too shallow, and Meta finds people who do cheap things. Choose one that's too rare, and Meta can't learn. Your skill is finding the right depth: deep enough to matter, and frequent enough to learn.

steps.p: An event only helps delivery if it reaches Meta quickly, with enough matching information to link it to a person who saw your ad. Each link in this chain can break, so test it before you spend.
steps.say: Follow this chain to see how a signal reaches Meta. A user acts. The pixel or your server sends the event. Meta matches it to a person who saw your ad. The event counts for the ad set. And delivery adjusts. An event only helps if it arrives quickly, with enough matching information. Each link in the chain can break, so test it before you spend.

steps.p: Example mapping for a trading funnel through a lander and Telegram. Use standard events where they fit, because Meta understands them by default. Custom events or custom conversions also work when nothing standard fits.
steps.say: Here's an example mapping for a trading funnel through a lander and Telegram. A lander view maps to View Content, with high volume. A Telegram join maps to Lead or a custom event, medium volume. A broker sign-up maps to Complete Registration, medium volume. And a first deposit maps to Purchase with value, low volume. Use standard events where they fit, because Meta understands them by default. Custom events work when nothing standard fits.

steps.p: If your funnel goes through Telegram, the join is often your best mid-funnel event. You need to count joins per invite link before you can send them as a Lead or custom event.

steps.h: Pixel only vs pixel plus Conversions API
steps.p: The pixel runs in the browser and can be blocked or lose cookies. The Conversions API sends events from your server or tracker. Using both, with matching event IDs, gives Meta more complete data.

a.title: Pixel only
items: Blocked by some browsers and apps
Cannot see events that happen later on the broker

steps.more: Full Conversions API and postback mapping: Tracking, advanced module. Beginner setup step by step: Tracking setup lab module.
steps.say: Compare the columns. The pixel only runs in the browser. It's easy to set up, but some browsers and apps block it, and it can't see events that happen later on the broker. Pixel plus Conversions A P I, application programming interface, sends events from both the browser and your server or tracker. It recovers events the pixel misses and can send F T Ds, first-time deposits, from postbacks. The catch: it needs deduplication.

steps.h: What a server event looks like
steps.p: A simplified example of one Conversions API event. Your tracker or server sends it when a postback says a deposit happened. Field names follow Meta's docs at the time of writing; we are not certain they are current, so check them before you build.

Most trackers build this for you once you map a postback goal to a Meta event; you mainly need to check the result in Events Manager.

steps.p: If the pixel and the server both send the same registration, Meta could count it twice. Send the same event name and the same event ID from both, and Meta keeps one. Check the deduplication status in Events Manager after setup; names change, so check the current tool.

steps.p: Multiply the expected cost per event by the events Meta wants per week, then divide by seven. This tells you whether an event is realistic for your daily budget before you build anything.
steps.say: So how do you know if an event is realistic? Look at the equation. Multiply the expected cost per event by fifty, the events Meta wants per week, then divide by seven days. That gives the daily budget one ad set needs. Do this before you build anything, and you'll know straight away whether your budget can feed that event.

steps.p: Example: costs per event in one trading funnel. Optimising for FTD gives the best users but needs about $214 a day per ad set to reach 50 a week. Registration needs $57. Choose what your budget can feed.

F T D gives the best users, but a buyer with sixty dollars a day should optimise for registration, judge on F T Ds in reporting, and test an F T D-optimised ad set as volume grows.

steps.p: Example: cost per FTD over seven weeks. The buyer optimised for registration first, then added an FTD-optimised ad set in week four once FTD volume was high enough. The deeper event found better depositors.

steps.p: Volume is not enough. Meta also needs to recognise who did the event. Better matching and honest values let it find more people like your real depositors.
steps.more: Events Manager shows a match quality score for server events. It improves when you send more of the identifiers users have consented to share, such as hashed email or phone, plus click ID and browser ID. Send only data you are allowed to collect under the privacy law of your geo and your own privacy policy.

steps.h: Never send fake or inflated events
steps.p: Some buyers fire events for people who did not act, or inflate values, to push delivery. It teaches Meta to find the wrong people, breaks platform terms, and corrupts your own data. Send only real events.

d.text: Every event you send must be a real action by a real person who agreed to your privacy terms.

steps.p: Meta gives you several ways to describe who should see your ads. At the time of writing, most of them are treated as suggestions that the system can expand beyond; check the current Ads Manager. Know what each one is for.
d: Lookalike|people similar to a seed list

steps.say: Meta gives you several ways to describe who should see your ads. Look at the cards. Broad uses location, age and gender only. Interests use detailed targeting by topic. Custom audiences are people who interacted with you. Lookalikes are people similar to a seed list. And an automated audience is one Meta builds from your suggestions. At the time of writing, most of these are treated as suggestions the system can expand beyond, so check the current Ads Manager.

steps.h: Your creative now does much of the targeting
steps.p: With broad audiences, Meta watches who stops, watches and converts on each ad, then finds more of them. A video in Pidgin about trading basics will find a different crowd from an English video about crypto. Your creative chooses the audience.

d.s: Who engages decides who Meta finds next

steps.say: Here's a big shift in how targeting works. With broad audiences, Meta watches who stops, watches and converts on each ad, then finds more of them. So a video in Pidgin about trading basics will find a different crowd from an English video about crypto. Your creative chooses the audience. Who engages decides who Meta finds next.

steps.p: Neither is always better. Broad gives Meta room to learn once your event and creative are strong. Interests can help a brand-new pixel find a starting point. Test both on the same creative.

a.title: Broad
items: Creative must call out the right people

steps.say: Neither broad nor interests is always better. Compare the columns. Broad gives a large pool, often at a lower C P M, cost per thousand impressions. It relies on strong event signal, needs creative that calls out the right people, and scales more easily. Interests give a smaller, defined pool that helps when signal is thin, but often costs more and can saturate faster. Test both on the same creative.

steps.h: Compare audiences on cost per result
steps.p: Cost per conversion depends on three numbers: CPM, CTR and conversion rate. Put them together and you can see why an audience with a higher CTR can still lose.
steps.say: To compare audiences fairly, look at cost per conversion, which depends on three numbers. C P M, C T R, that's click-through rate, and conversion rate. Look at the equation: C P M divided by one thousand times C T R times conversion rate gives cost per conversion. Putting them together shows why an audience with a higher C T R can still lose.

steps.p: Example: same creative, same offer, same week. The interest ad set had a higher CTR, but broad delivered at a lower CPM, so broad won on cost per registration.
steps.more: Worked example. Interests: $3.50 ÷ (1,000 × 0.015 × 0.02) = $3.50 ÷ 0.30 = $11.67. Broad: $2.20 ÷ (1,000 × 0.012 × 0.02) = $2.20 ÷ 0.24 = $9.17. Here CR is click to registration. Always finish with your real paid event too: if broad registrations deposit less often, the answer can flip.
steps.say: Here's a worked example, same creative, same offer, same week. Read the table. Interests had a C P M of three fifty and a C T R of one point five percent. Broad had a C P M of two twenty and a C T R of one point two percent. Both converted two percent of clicks to registrations. The result: eleven sixty seven per registration for interests, nine seventeen for broad. Broad won on cost. But always finish with your real paid event, because if broad registrations deposit less often, the answer can flip.

lessons.title: Automation, placements and the learning phase
objectives: By the end you can decide when to use automated campaign options and when to keep manual control.
You can read placement breakdowns and act on them.
You can avoid edits that reset learning and know what 'learning limited' means.
You can apply a starting rule before cutting a placement.

steps.h: Automation is a tool, not a strategy
steps.p: Meta keeps adding automated options under the Advantage name: automated campaigns, audiences, placements, budgets and creative enhancements. Names change; check the current Ads Manager. They often work well with strong signal. They still need clear inputs, honest creative and your judgement.
steps.say: Meta keeps adding automated options under the Advantage name: automated campaigns, audiences, placements, budgets and creative enhancements. Names change, so check the current Ads Manager. They often work well with strong signal. But they still need clear inputs, honest creative and your judgement. Automate the delivery, but keep control of the rules.

steps.p: Automated campaign types reduce the number of settings and let Meta move budget between audiences, placements and ads. Manual setups are slower but easier to read when you are testing.

a.title: Automated campaign types
items: Harder to see why results change

steps.say: Compare the two setups. Automated campaign types have fewer settings and let Meta move budget freely between audiences, placements and ads. They're strong when signal is good, but it's harder to see why results change. Manual campaigns have more settings to control and take more work, but they give clean tests of one variable and are easier to diagnose. That's why manual setups suit testing.

steps.p: Some automated options can change your creative: adjust brightness, add music, crop images, add text or generate variations. For regulated offers, review what is switched on so nothing alters your claims or removes a required warning.

d.text: Review enhancement settings on every new ad. Turn off any that could change claims or hide risk text.

steps.h: Starting rule for cutting a placement
steps.p: Do not cut a placement on one day of data. Starting rule: exclude or separately test a placement only once it has spent at least 3 × your target and its cost per paid event is above your kill line. Adapt to your data.
steps.more: The kill line is the lower of 1.5 × target and break-even, the same as the ad set rule card. Here 1.5 × $10 = $15 and break-even is $14, so the line is $14. Full rule card: Budget and kill rules module.

d.text: Example: target $10 per registration, break-even $14. Audience Network spent $90 (9 × target) at $30 per registration over 7 days: cut it.

steps.say: Here's a starting rule for cutting a placement. Exclude it, or test it separately, only once it has spent at least three times your target, and its cost per paid event is above your kill line. In this example, the target is ten dollars per registration and break-even is fourteen. Audience Network spent ninety dollars, nine times target, at thirty dollars per registration over seven days. So it's cut. Adapt the rule to your data.

steps.p: After you launch or significantly edit an ad set, Meta explores who converts. Costs swing and results are less stable. Once it has enough conversions, delivery settles. Your job during learning is mostly patience.

d.s: Results swing until Meta has enough data

steps.say: After you launch or significantly edit an ad set, Meta explores who converts. That's the learning phase. Costs swing and results are less stable. Once it has enough conversions, delivery settles. Your job during learning is mostly patience. Explore, then settle.

steps.p: Example: daily cost per registration for a new ad set. It swings for the first days while Meta explores, then settles. The second line shows what happens when the buyer edits the ad set on day three.

steps.p: Automation hides some decisions from you. These mistakes happen when buyers forget that, or fight the learning phase instead of planning around it. Each fix below keeps your data readable and your spend under control.

b.title: Fixes
items: Consolidate or move the event up

steps.say: Automation hides some decisions from you. These mistakes come from forgetting that, or fighting the learning phase. The fixes: review enhancements on every ad instead of leaving them on blindly. Spend three times target before cutting a placement, not one day. Batch edits and log each one, instead of editing daily. Consolidate or move the event up when learning is limited. And test manually, then scale with automation.

steps.p: Simple habits that keep your ad sets stable while Meta learns. They also keep your data clean enough to make real decisions at the end of a test.
d: Do not edit for the first few days unless something is broken
Add new creative in a planned slot
Write every change in a log
steps.say: Finally, simple habits that keep ad sets stable while Meta learns. Decide kill rules before launch. Don't edit for the first few days unless something's broken. Batch edits into one change. Add new creative in a planned slot. And write every change in a log. These habits also keep your data clean enough to make real decisions at the end of a test.

lessons.title: Budgets, bidding and automated rules
objectives: By the end you can choose between campaign and ad set budgets.
You can explain the main bid strategies and when to use each.

steps.h: Campaign budget vs ad set budget
steps.p: With a campaign budget, Meta spreads money across ad sets based on where it expects results. With ad set budgets, you decide how much each one gets. Meta's name for campaign budget has changed over time; check the current Ads Manager.

a.title: Campaign budget
items: Some ad sets may get almost nothing

b.title: Ad set budget
items: You control each ad set's spend

steps.say: Compare the two budget types. With a campaign budget, Meta moves money to winners. It's less manual work and good for scaling proven setups, but some ad sets may get almost nothing. With ad set budgets, you control each ad set's spend. It's more work, but gives fair tests between audiences, so it's good for testing. Meta's name for campaign budget has changed over time, so check the current Ads Manager.

steps.p: Meta has said it may spend more than your daily budget on good days and less on others, while keeping weekly spend within a set limit. We are not certain of the exact rule today; check current docs, and plan cash flow on the weekly figure.
steps.more: Meta's help pages have described spending up to 75% above a daily budget on some days, while keeping spend over a calendar week at or below seven times the daily budget. Treat this as an example of the mechanism and confirm the current rule. If your bank card or credit line is tight, set limits at account level too.

d.text: Plan spend by the week. A $50 daily budget can spend more than $50 on some days.

steps.say: Here's something that catches beginners out. Meta has said it may spend more than your daily budget on good days and less on others, while keeping weekly spend within a set limit. Its help pages have described up to seventy five percent above a daily budget on some days. We're not certain of the exact rule today, so check current docs. The practical point: plan by the week, because a fifty dollar daily budget can spend more than fifty on some days.

steps.p: Bid strategies tell Meta how to balance volume and cost. These are the common types with their names at the time of writing in brackets. Names change; check the current Ads Manager. The ideas behind them have stayed similar.

rows: Gets most results for the budget
Aims to keep average cost near a target
Limits the bid in each auction
Aims for a minimum return on value

steps.say: Bid strategies tell Meta how to balance volume and cost. Read the table. Highest volume, or lowest cost, gets the most results for the budget, for testing and most cases. Cost per result goal, or cost cap, aims to keep average cost near a target, when you know your max C P A, cost per acquisition. Bid cap limits the bid in each auction, for strict control by experienced buyers. And R O A S goal, return on ad spend, aims for a minimum return when you send real values.

steps.h: Setting a cost goal from the offer
steps.p: Start a cost goal from what a result is worth to you, not from a number you saw online. Example: a registration is worth $12, you want a 25% margin, so the goal is $9.
steps.say: Start a cost goal from what a result is worth to you, not from a number you saw online. Look at the equation. In this example, a registration is worth twelve dollars and you want a twenty five percent margin. Twelve dollars times seventy five percent gives a nine dollar cost goal.

steps.p: Example: daily spend on two ad sets with a $100 budget. One has a realistic cost goal, one has a goal far below the market cost. The tight one barely spends, so it learns nothing.
steps.more: Worked example. Market cost per registration is around $10. Ad set A's goal is $10 and it spends close to budget. Ad set B's goal is $5. Meta cannot find many registrations at $5, so it spends $12 to $20 a day. Over a week B gets a handful of cheap results and no scale. If an ad set with a cost goal under-spends, raise the goal in small steps or go back to highest volume.
steps.say: Here's what happens when a cost goal is too tight. In this example, two ad sets each have a one hundred dollar budget. The top line has a realistic ten dollar goal and spends close to budget every day. The bottom line has a five dollar goal, far below the market cost of around ten. It barely spends, twelve to twenty dollars a day, so it learns nothing. If an ad set with a cost goal under-spends, raise the goal in small steps or go back to highest volume.

steps.p: Large budget jumps can act like a significant edit and unsettle delivery. Starting rule: raise by 20%, at least 48 hours apart, only while CPA ≤ 0.8 × target with 3 or more network-confirmed conversions. The 20% is a habit, not a Meta rule.
steps.more: Worked example. Start at $100 a day. Each step adds 20%: $120, $144, $172.80, $207.36. With 48 hours between steps, the earliest you reach $207.36 is about day 9, and each step has to be earned again with CPA since the step at or under 0.8 × target. If CPA rises above target after a step, stop stepping, and go back to the last budget that worked. Full scaling rules: Budget and kill rules module.

d.note: Starting rule. Earned with CPA ≤ 0.8 × target and 3+ conversions.

The twenty percent is a habit, not a Meta rule. Each step has to be earned again. If C P A rises above target after a step, stop, and go back to the last budget that worked.

exam.q: You have $70 a day for a new trading offer. Registration costs about $10 and FTD about $45. Which setup fits?
options: Optimise for FTD in 5 ad sets
Optimise for registration in 1 to 2 ad sets and judge on FTDs
exam.why: FTD at $45 × 50 ÷ 7 needs about $321 a day. Registration at $10 needs about $71. One or two registration ad sets fit the budget.

exam.q: Ad set A: CPM $5, CTR 2%, click-to-reg 2.5%. Ad set B: CPM $3, CTR 1%, click-to-reg 2.5%. Which has the lower cost per registration?
Events Manager shows registrations counted twice since you added the Conversions API. What is the likely fix?
options: Send the same event name and event ID from both pixel and server
exam.why: Matching event names and IDs let Meta deduplicate the browser and server copies.

exam.q: Ads Manager shows 10 Purchases on $200 spend; the network confirms 5 qualified FTDs. Target $30, break-even $40, postbacks matured. What do the starting rules say?
options: Hold: the network CPA of $40 is not above the $40 kill line
Scale, the Ads Manager CPA is $20
Kill, the CPA is above target
exam.why: Decide on network numbers: $200 ÷ 5 = $40. The kill line is the lower of $45 and $40, so $40. CPA must be above it to kill, so the card says Hold, and the ad set needs work before any budget.

exam.q: A placement breakdown over 7 days: Audience Network $120 spend, 900 clicks, 2 FTDs. Feeds $400 spend, 16 FTDs. Target cost per FTD $30. What is reasonable?
options: Move all budget to Audience Network for cheap clicks
Exclude or separately test Audience Network; it costs $60 per FTD vs $25
exam.why: Audience Network: $120 ÷ 2 = $60 per FTD. Feeds: $400 ÷ 16 = $25. Act on the paid event, with enough data.

exam.q: A gambling campaign's automated audience is turned on. What must you still confirm?
options: That minimum age and location are set as firm limits within your licence and permission
exam.why: Age and location for regulated offers are legal limits. Confirm they cannot be expanded.

exam.q: You raise a winning ad set from $100 to $400 a day in one step and costs double. What do the starting rules say you should have done?
options: Raise +20% at a time, at least 48 h apart, while CPA stays ≤ 0.8 × target with 3+ conversions
exam.why: Big jumps can act like a significant edit. +20% steps, each earned, let you watch cost at every level.

exam.q: A rule pauses any ad set with zero FTDs after spending $40. Target cost per FTD is $35 and FTDs often arrive two days late. What is wrong?
options: The rule fires on incomplete FTD data and will kill ad sets that would have converted
exam.why: Meta cannot see late postbacks yet. Use rules on fast events and review FTDs with complete data.

exam.q: Target $9 per registration. Which automated rule matches the starting stop loss?
options: Pause any ad set with CTR under 1%
Pause at $18 spent with 0 registrations today
exam.why: The zero-conversion kill rule is spend ≥ 2 × target with no results: 2 × $9 = $18. Registrations are fast enough for a rule to use.

exam.q: A value per FTD is $50, you want a 30% margin and you use a cost per result goal. Spend is low at a $25 goal. What is a sensible change?
options: Raise the goal in steps towards $35
exam.why: Your break-even with a 30% margin is $50 × 0.70 = $35. A $25 goal is below what you can afford and is choking delivery.
